description: Which abandoned packages are NOT worth flagging, and why each one earned it.
Split out of default.json so a project can take the verdicts without taking
this org's behaviour with them. it-tools wants the exclusions and keeps its
own pinning, soak and grouping; a fork wants both. One list, two audiences,
and a new repo inherits the reasoning instead of re-deriving it -- which is
the whole value as the number of repos grows.
THE TEST, applied per package and strictly. An abandonment flag earns its
place because an unmaintained package stops refreshing its dependency tree,
and that tree rots and collects CVEs. A package that declares nothing has no
tree to rot, so the flag names no action. Declaring ANY runtime, peer or
optional dependency disqualifies a package -- even one whose dependency is
current today, because a dependency is the thing that can age.
Being 'on latest' is not sufficient, and neither is being small. Anything
abandoned that ships a runtime tree must be OWNED -- forked, vendored or
replaced -- never silenced.
A direct CVE is still surfaced: this silences only the age-based flag, and
vulnerability alerts are configured in default.json, not here.

packageRules.description: Suppress abandonment flags only for abandoned zero-dependency leaf clones we neither ship to consumers nor plan to fork or vendor - pure dashboard noise, nothing to act on. Anything abandoned that ships in a published @unabandoned tree (e.g. ret) or that we vendor or intend to fork stays flagged (save for the reviewed frozen-leaf exception in the next rule), because that is an actionable signal we do not want to hide.

Suppress abandonment flags only for abandoned packages that declare ZERO runtime dependencies of their own and are frozen at their latest release - there is nothing under them to rot, so the flag carries no actionable signal (a direct CVE is still surfaced by the vulnerabilityAlerts above). Eligibility is strict and per-package: declaring ANY runtime dependency disqualifies a package - even if that dependency is itself current or separately suppressed here - and it must be owned (fork, vendor, or replace) rather than silenced. Being 'on latest' is not sufficient. These ship in, or are dev deps of, @unabandoned/browser-pack, @unabandoned/module-deps, @unabandoned/jsonstream and @unabandoned/browserify: jsonparse is the sole runtime leaf of @unabandoned/jsonstream (pulled transitively by browser-pack, module-deps, deps-sort and insert-module-globals); through is now only a dev dependency of @unabandoned/browserify (JSONStream's old runtime through was vendored into @unabandoned/jsonstream when it was forked 2026-08, so it no longer ships in the runtime tree). Reviewed 2026-08.

Suppress abandonment flags for the abandoned zero-runtime-dep leaves that ship in (or are dev deps of) @unabandoned/browserify and @unabandoned/module-deps: node-builtin browser-polyfill shims (console-browserify, constants-browserify, https-browserify, os-browserify, tty-browserify, vm-browserify, process, punycode, querystring-es3, inherits) and small internal/test leaves (cached-path-relative, defined, has-object-spread, has-template-literals, isstream). Each declares zero runtime dependencies of its own, so there is nothing under them to rot; a direct CVE is still surfaced by the vulnerabilityAlerts above. The has-runtime-dep polyfills (stream-browserify, util, url, stream-http, browserify-zlib, timers-browserify, readable-stream) and crypto-browserify are deliberately NOT listed here - carrying a runtime dependency, they must be owned (fork/vendor/replace), not silenced. safe-buffer (frozen at 5.2.1, 2020-05-10) joins them: zero runtime dependencies, and it ships in @unabandoned/browserify-sign, @unabandoned/crypto-browserify and several of the browserify leaves. hash-test-vectors (frozen at 1.3.2, 2015-01-14) joins them: zero runtime dependencies, and it is a devDependency holding the node-produced digest corpus @unabandoned/crypto-browserify checks its hash implementations against - fixture data, not code, with nothing beneath it to rot. Reviewed 2026-09.

Suppress abandonment flags for the abandoned zero-runtime-dep leaves that ship in @unabandoned/undeclared-identifiers: dash-ast (frozen at 2.0.1, 2020-03-11) and get-assigned-identifiers (frozen at 1.2.0, 2018-02-08). Both declare zero runtime dependencies of their own, so there is nothing under them to rot and the flag carries no actionable signal; a direct CVE is still surfaced by the vulnerabilityAlerts above. Their own devDependencies are stale (acorn 5/7, standard 10/14, tape 4) but are never installed by consumers and never run in our CI, so forking would create that dev-tree exposure rather than remove it. simple-concat, the third package the dashboard flagged on this fork, is deliberately NOT listed here - it was a one-call stdin slurp replaced outright by the built-in node:stream/consumers, so it left the tree instead of being silenced. Reviewed 2026-08.

Suppress abandonment flags for pluralize (frozen at 8.0.0, 2019-05-25), the one inert leaf that ships in @unabandoned/json-to-ts: it declares zero runtime dependencies of its own, so there is nothing under it to rot and the flag carries no actionable signal; a direct CVE is still surfaced by the vulnerabilityAlerts above. The other two packages json-to-ts's dashboard flagged are deliberately NOT listed here, because neither was silenced: es7-shim left the tree outright (everything it polyfilled is native now), and hash.js declares runtime dependencies of its own, so it was adopted as @unabandoned/hash.js - which in turn vendored its own two leaves (minimalistic-assert, inherits: ten and fifteen lines of ISC code) instead of depending on them, so neither is in any tree of ours to suppress. Reviewed 2026-09.

description: Inert leaves in the PROJECTS this preset serves, as opposed to the
@unabandoned/* trees the rules above cover. Same test, same reasoning,
different consumer -- a project extending this should inherit the verdict
rather than re-deriving it, which is why the list lives here.
Each was checked at the version the consuming project pins, not at latest:
zero dependencies, zero peerDependencies, zero optionalDependencies.

Reviewed 2026-10-03 for it-tools, where eleven abandonment flags were hiding the four that needed acting on; @vicons/material added on the same date from the same dashboard (0.13.0, frozen 2024-12-20, zero dependencies, supplies the icon components in every tool's index.ts).
The inert leaves on @unabandoned/qrcode's dashboard. Same test as the rules above,
checked per package at the version the fork pins, not at latest:
canvasutil  0.0.4, frozen 2014-05-26 - dev only, used by examples/clientsideserver.js,
and examples/ is not in package.json#files, so it reaches no consumer.
dijkstrajs  1.0.3, frozen 2023-04-15 - runtime, required by lib/core/segments.js.
pngjs       7.0.0, frozen 2023-02-20 - runtime, required by lib/renderer/png.js.
All three declare zero dependencies, zero peerDependencies and zero
optionalDependencies, so there is nothing under them to rot and the flag names no
action. Two of them ship, which is not disqualifying on its own - the frozen-leaf
exception turns on the tree, not on the audience - and a direct CVE in any of them
is still surfaced by the vulnerabilityAlerts in default.json.
The other three packages qrcode's dashboard flagged are deliberately NOT here,
because none of them was silenced: browserify and colors left the tree outright
(declared devDependencies that nothing in the repository required), and standard
declares nine dependencies of its own headed by an end-of-life eslint 8, so it was
replaced with neostandard, its maintained successor.
Reviewed 2026-10-03.
A GitHub Action, not an npm package, so none of the rules above can reach it:
they all match the npm datasource.
amannn/action-semantic-pull-request validates PR titles against Conventional
Commits in it-tools. Renovate flags it because its last RELEASE was 2025-08-22,
and the dashboard says plainly how it decides: 'abandonment is detected by
release inactivity'. That is the wrong signal here. The repository had commits
two days before this rule was written, it is not archived, and the work in them
is routine dependency maintenance on a 1.4k-star action that has been feature
complete for a year. Nothing is rotting; nobody has walked away.
It is also pinned by commit SHA with the version in a comment, so what runs in
CI cannot change under us, and Renovate still offers digest and version updates
for it -- this silences only the age-based flag.
Reviewed 2026-10-03.
